title: CHRPE: The Definitive Clinical Guide
summary: Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (CHRPE) is a benign but clinically significant pigmented fundus lesion. While usually solitary and harmless, specific phenotypic variations serve as a critical 'red flag' for life-threatening systemic malignancies like Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concepts
sections.content: CHRPE is a congenital hamartoma characterized by a localized increase in the size of RPE cells (hypertrophy) rather than an increase in the number of cells (hyperplasia). These cells are packed with large, spherical melanin granules known as macromelanosomes. Clinically, it presents as a flat, sharply demarcated, hyperpigmented lesion often containing characteristic depigmented lacunae.

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Color: Slate-gray to jet-black
Shape: Round or oval with crisp, sharp margins
Lacunae: Well-circumscribed areas of depigmentation (enlarge over time)
Halo: Hypopigmented rim often surrounds the lesion
Elevation: Always FLAT (cannot be detected by B-scan ultrasound)
Location: Usually mid-periphery or periphery

rows: RPE thickening, overlying photoreceptor loss, posterior shadowing
Flat; No internal reflectivity; No thickness

sections.title: RED FLAG: Gardner Syndrome & FAP
content: Atypical CHRPE is often the FIRST sign of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).
Lesions are typically bilateral, multiple (>3), and spindle-shaped (Pisciform).
Associated with APC gene mutation on Chromosome 5q21.
100% risk of colon cancer by age 50 if untreated.
Gardner Syndrome Triad: FAP, Osteomas (mandible/skull), and Soft tissue tumors (Desmoid).

sections.title: Symptomatology & Functional Deficits
content: Usually asymptomatic (discovered on routine exam)
Absolute Scotoma corresponds exactly to the lesion area
Reduced contrast sensitivity (rarely noticed by patient)
No effect on visual acuity unless the lesion involves the fovea (extremely rare)

sections.title: Management & Follow-up Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform dilated fundus exam and baseline photography.
Step 2: Assess for 'Atypical' features (bilaterality, pisciform shape).
Step 3: If solitary/grouped: Annual monitoring for growth/change.
Step 4: If atypical: Immediate referral to Gastroenterology for Colonoscopy.
Step 5: Genetic counseling for APC gene mutations if FAP suspected.

content.explanation: F: Flat (no elevation on USG); L: Lacunae (depigmented windows); A: APC Gene (association with FAP); T: Tall RPE cells (hypertrophy).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Lacunae tend to enlarge and coalesce over many years.
CHRPE is 'silent' on FFA except for the lacunae which show window defects.
Unlike nevi, CHRPE does not typically have overlying drusen.
Bear tracks (Grouped CHRPE) are NEVER associated with Gardner Syndrome.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
sections.content: Prognosis for vision is excellent. While slow growth occurs in up to 25% of cases over decades, malignant transformation into an RPE Adenocarcinoma is extremely rare but documented. Such transformation presents as a nodular growth with associated exudation or hemorrhage.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
content: Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI-OCT) confirms CHRPE is confined to the RPE layer.
Studies show that even a single pisciform lesion should prompt FAP screening in the right clinical context.
FAP-associated lesions are found in approximately 70-90% of patients with the condition.
